catalog_quote: 3.5.1. Lexical stress. The stress in Qashqai words is a final high pitch, both in nominals, ex. áγ ‘white’, aγáǰ ‘wood’, mašḯn ‘car’, emtehán ‘exam’, and in verb stems, ex. ergán- ‘learn’, qäreštér- ‘mix’. In compound words, the stress falls on the final syllable of the second component, as in, beyίn < bu gin ‘today’, baš-aγrḯ ‘headache’, at-quyruγú ‘horse-tail’, sarï-darmán ‘curry’. [...] 3.5.2.1. Stressable suffixes. Most suffixes in Qashqai are stressable. [...] i) With monosyllabic suffixes such as the plural suffix –LAr, most of derivational suffixes, and most of case suffixes, the stress falls on the suffixal syllable, ex. daš-lár ‘stones’, iran-lḯ, ‘Iranian’, šähr-dá ‘in Shiraz’. [...] iii) Multiple suffixation: when the root is attached to more than one stressable suffix, the stress moves to the stressable syllable of the last suffix, ex. širaz-däy-lǟr ‘those (who) are in Shiraz…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (realized as a high pitch) falls on the final syllable of the word, including the last stressable suffix; a closed class of suffixes (copula, personal endings, negation -mA, equative -čä) and Persian clitics never take stress, so stress stays on the syllable before them. Corroborated independently by Çelik 1997: 82, 'Kaşkay Türkçesi metinlerinde vurgu umumiyetle son hecededir' (in the Kashkay texts stress is generally on the last syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressable suffixes: copular -DI, -(y)IdI, -(y)ImIš; personal suffixes -äm, -äη, -äG, -äηiz; equative -čä; negation -mA; Persian indefinite clitic =i (stress is the only cue separating it from the stressed accusative -(y)i). Disyllabic instrumental -(y/I)nän and terminative -(y)AnčA are stressed on their first syllable (pre-final); -(y)IηIz and -(y)akï on their last. Aorist negative -mäz is stressed (ged-mǟz-dig). Author explicitly models stress and intonation on Persian (Lazard 2006).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('lexical stress', §3.5.1-2); a separate §3.5.3 'Prosodic stress' says phrase/clause stress is as in Persian, with finite verb forms and verb-final groups stressed on a non-final syllable; sentence intonation falling in declaratives/wh-questions, rising in yes/no questions (no interrogative particle). Grammar mainly treats the Amaleh variety (p. 5, §2.4.1).
new_statements.identity_note: Dolatkhah 2019 states (p. 5, §2.4.1) that the grammar mainly treats the Amaleh-tribe variety of Qashqai (qash1240 proper); Çelik 1997 is based on texts from Qashqai proper too. Kowalski 1937, listed by Glottolog under qash1240, actually describes Äinallu (Aynallu), which Kowalski himself (pp. 67-68) treats as a distinct South Oghuz dialect from Qashqai; it contains no stress statement anyway.
